newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German tax panels set, industry urges cuts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German tax panels set, industry urges cuts.

text.p: The German parliament's mediation committee on Thursday set up working groups to seek compromise on a package of income tax cuts and agreed to meet again later this month.

"The working groups will be set up and then we will see how things are at the end of July," Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on the sidelines of the meeting of representatives of government and opposition parties.

Participants said Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition of Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) and Free Democrats (FDP) would meet opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and environmentalist Greens for tax talks on July 28 and 29.
German industry, meanwhile, urged the parties involved in the tax reform negotiations to do their utmost to lighten the tax burden.

Germany levies some of the highest income and company taxes in the world. The reform initially set out to cut these by 30 billion marks ($17 billion) to help boost flagging investment at home and stop jobs being exported abroad.
Low tax revenues and high unemployment outlays are the main factors seen boosting the 1997 budget deficit to 71 billion marks from an earlier estimate of 53.3 billion.
Waigel hopes tax cuts are the best way to get the economy in shape for European economic and monetary union.

The lower house of parliament, or Bundestag, passed two tax bills last month that would introduce up to 30 billion marks in income tax cuts over the next two years, close loopholes and make changes to corporate tax rules.

But the main opposition SPD, which governs in a majority of federal states and thus has control of the upper house, or Bundesrat, blocked final passage and the government called on the mediation committee to seek a compromise.

The German Federation of Chambers of Commerce (DIHT), Federation of German Industry (BDI), Federation of Employers' Associations (BDA) and the Federation of Skilled Craftsmen and Tradesmen (ZDH) warned both sides their decision was crucial to whether Germany would be competitive again in future.

"From industry's point of view, if the tax reform fails in parliamentary mediation, it will have drastic consequences for companies' willingness to invest in Germany and will scare off foreign investors even more," the four groups said in a joint statement issued by the ZDH.

Prospects looked dim for a compromise, mediation committee chairman Heribert Blens earlier told German Radio in Berlin, while adding that there were some areas where the sides showed potential for agreement.

"The abolition of capital tax for companies is one bill which we on the mediation committee have discussed for a long time. I am optimistic that we will reach a good result on this," Blens said in an interview.
Blens said there was also a chance of making progress on proposals to reduce non-labour wage costs -- one of the factors that makes labour in western Germany the most expensive in the world.
Blens noted the SPD were keen on reducing non-labour wage costs but that the problem was that the government bill linked this with pension and unemployment benefit reforms.

"The SPD in their draft legislation want to counter-balance this reduction by raising valued added tax (VAT) and fuel tax each by one percentage point," he said. "I think we can make a little progress here because both sides' proposals lead to a reduction in non-labour costs."
Kohl's FDP coalition partners, self-styled champions of tax-cutting, have ruled out a reform involving tax hikes to finance other reductions.
FDP parliamentary leader Hermann-Otto Solms told Berlin's InfoRadio his party, on which Kohl relies for his 12-seat majority, was not going to change its tough position on this.
"It is unacceptable to come up with a re-distribution which means taxpayers, who already pay too much, should come out of this empty-handed," Solms said in an interview.

"All the experts say we need a reduction in taxes and social and health contributions to create a better investment climate. Jobs can only be created through investment," he said. ($ = 1.763 German Marks)
